column3: Description
A single‑line box where users can type anything from names to short notes.
A secure text box that masks what users type so others can’t read the password.
A text box that checks for a valid @‑formatted address as the user types.
Up‑ and down‑arrow controls that let users nudge a numeric value one step at a time.
A text box with a magnifying‑glass icon for quick look‑ups.
A larger box that lets users write paragraphs, comments, or longer messages.
A formatting toolbar and text field where users can bold, list, or link their content.
A small square that users tick or untick to say “yes” or “no” to an option.
A set of round options where choosing one automatically unselects the others.
A sliding on/off control that works like a light switch for settings.
A collapsed list that opens to reveal choices, then shows the one picked.
A dropdown that lets users choose several items and often shows them as tags.
A mini calendar pop‑up for selecting a specific day without typing.
Two linked calendars that capture a start and end date in one smooth interaction.
A scroll or dial control where users choose an exact hour and minute.
A palette or slider that lets users pick any shade and returns its hex value.
Opens the device’s file browser so users can attach documents or images.
A dashed‑border box where users simply drag files in to start uploading.
A horizontal bar with a knob users slide to pick a value like volume or brightness.
A compact field with “+” and “–” buttons that increment numbers cleanly.
An input that turns typed words into small pill‑shaped tags.
Starts suggesting results as the user types, saving time and reducing typos.
Pulls real street suggestions while typing so addresses are accurate and fast.
Combines a flag dropdown with a masked phone field to capture numbers correctly.
Automatically adds currency symbols and thousand separators while the user types.
Spaces digits in the right pattern and shows the card type as soon as it’s recognized.
A small month‑and‑year dropdown pair tailored for credit‑card expiry dates.
A tiny masked box for the 3‑ or 4‑digit security code on payment cards.
A “I’m not a robot” box that reduces spam with a single click.
Runs quietly in the background to verify humans without extra steps.
Stores behind‑the‑scenes values that a form needs but users don’t change.
Lets users tap one to five stars to rate products or experiences.
Pops up a browsable set of emojis and inserts the chosen one into text.
A colored bar that judges how strong the typed password is in real time.
A required tick box used for terms of service or privacy consent.
Formats sensitive numbers (like SSNs) with helpful dashes while typing.
Validates that the entry begins with http:// or https:// for working links.
A split‑view box where users write markdown and see a live preview.
A blank canvas where users draw their signature with a mouse or finger.
A simple two‑state switch labeled “Yes” and “No” for binary decisions.
Lets users resize and crop a picture before saving it.
Users drag two knobs to set a minimum and maximum value, like price range.
Shows numbered steps and highlights the current one to guide multi‑page forms.
Two radio buttons (“Allow” / “Deny”) used for permissions or preferences.
Hides sensitive tokens until the user clicks “Show” to copy them.
Displays a thumbnail or filename of uploaded files before the form is sent.
Six small boxes that each hold one digit of a one‑time passcode.
A slider that snaps to fixed points, showing small ticks for each step.
Shows how many characters remain as users type tweets or SMS messages.
Lets users add or remove identical input rows, like multiple email addresses.
The label starts as placeholder text and smoothly floats above once the user begins typing.
Real‑time feedback that appears right beneath an input to show errors like “Email required.”
A text box that shows a small icon (e.g., @ or $) inside the field to hint at expected content.
Places an icon (like an eye or calendar) at the end of the field to clarify its purpose.
Adds an “×” button inside the search box so users can wipe text in one click.
Waits a short moment after typing stops before firing the search, cutting server calls.
Grows taller automatically as the user writes, so no scroll bars appear.
Shows the maximum allowed characters and counts down while the user types.
Lets users pick a profile photo and instantly shows a circular preview.
Opens a simple crop tool so users can trim and zoom photos before saving.
Displays a live bar that fills up as the chosen file uploads.
Accepts several files at once and lists each with its own progress indicator.
Splits large files into smaller chunks to improve reliability on slow networks.
Activates the camera, reads a QR code, and autofills the decoded text.
Uses the device camera to read barcodes and drop the value into an input.
A microphone button that converts spoken words into text in real time.
Opens an interactive map where users drop a pin and the address fills automatically.
A yes/no toggle asking permission to use the device’s current location.
Captures precise latitude and longitude when users click a point on the map.
A horizontal bar where users drag a knob to select a score between 1 and 10.
Presents five labeled buttons (Strongly Disagree → Strongly Agree) for quick surveys.
Uses expressive face icons to let users choose their mood or satisfaction level.
Shows numbers 0‑10 in a row for easy NPS feedback.
A pill‑shaped bar divided into two or three segments acting like exclusive tabs.
A square card that toggles on/off when clicked, much larger than a standard checkbox.
A rounded pill that slides left/right to represent off/on states.
An eye icon that reveals or hides password characters on demand.
Creates a random strong password and drops it into the field with one click.
A masked multiline box for sensitive notes—content stays blurred until “Show” is tapped.
Small, rounded chips where selecting one deselects the rest—great for categories.
Chips that stay active as you tap additional ones, perfect for tag selection.
A vertical list of checkboxes plus a top option that toggles every item.
A compact field where users type a date in MM/DD/YYYY format with auto‑slashes.
Lists regions like “GMT+3 — Nairobi” so users can pick their local zone.
Shows a searchable list of countries, often with flags for quick visual scanning.
Populates a second dropdown after country is chosen, narrowing to local regions.
Lets users drag two ends to set a minimum and maximum spend range.
Combines two color pickers and a preview bar to craft smooth gradients.
Opens the device gallery and allows selecting multiple photos at once.
Limits selectable files to specific types like PDFs or images before browsing.
An invisible input that traps bots—if it’s filled, the form flags as spam.
Shows a small jigsaw‑style image puzzle users slide together to prove they’re human.
Six tidy boxes that auto‑move focus as each digit of an OTP is entered.
A tiny badge next to the field that updates with remaining characters.
Adds or removes identical input rows—useful for extra phone numbers or links.
Displays numbered steps across the top and highlights the current one in multi‑page forms.
A small “?” icon that reveals extra guidance when hovered or tapped.
Pops a short explanation bubble beside the field without leaving the page.
Shows how the entered street, city, and zip will look on a mailing label in real time.
Automatically adds commas and decimal places while typing amounts.
Lets users drag list items up or down to define a custom order within the form.
A colored bar at the top of the page that lists every validation mistake after submission and links users back to each field.
A small pop‑up that briefly appears in the corner confirming the form was saved or sent.
An automatic red asterisk (with aria‑required) added to labels so users know which inputs are mandatory.
A hidden text label that pairs with icon‑only inputs to keep them understandable for assistive technology.
A visual box that groups related inputs under a titled legend like “Billing Address.”
An accordion panel that hides or reveals long sets of fields, keeping multi‑step forms tidy.
A grid where each row is a statement and each column is a rating option (e.g., 1–5), so surveys stay compact.
An editable table that lets users type straight into cells to add multiple rows of data quickly.
Forces an MM/DD/YYYY pattern and auto‑inserts slashes so dates are always valid.
Guides users to enter hours and minutes in HH:MM format, adding the colon for them.
Automatically capitalizes letters and adds the right spacing for locale‑specific ZIP or post codes.
